summary: Each round you play a card whose suit either wins you a trick (and influence in a town toward area majority) or, if you lose it, lets you take a strong action like recruiting, building a monastery, or arranging a marriage. The tension between wanting to win tricks for board position and wanting to lose them for tempo-defining actions makes for a tight, cerebral, high-interaction game that plays out more like a control-point puzzle than a typical trick-taker.
praised: Genuinely novel twist on trick-taking where losing a trick is often as valuable as winning it
Tight, interlocking systems with little wasted design space
High player interaction through area majority fights over towns and regions
Strong theme integration of the three historical pillars (war, church, marriage) into the three suits
Rewards planning and reading opponents' hands/intentions
criticised: Steep learning curve and rules overhead for a card game, with a lot to track on the first few plays
Some players find the trick-taking layer fiddly when combined with area control bookkeeping
Can feel swingy or luck-influenced when a bad hand of cards limits your options
Downtime/analysis paralysis at higher player counts as everyone evaluates trick implications
Iconography and the town/region map take real effort to parse before the game clicks

interaction.kind: area majority fights over towns/regions plus direct trick-taking confrontation

win_criteria: Most points, one or two sources

scoring.why: Victory is driven primarily by controlling towns and regions through trick-won influence, with actions from lost tricks serving mainly to set up or defend that majority control
